title: Overview and justification
body:
This short course is about the craft of finding sources: how to search well, not just how to search. By the end you will be able to plan a search before you begin, build the keywords and synonyms that drive it, and construct and refine a real search in your library discovery service using Boolean logic and limiters.

Searching is one of the most important academic skills, and most students do it far less effectively than they could. A planned, well-built search finds better sources in less time, and better sources make better work. This course turns searching from guesswork into a strategy you control.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: plan a search by setting clear objectives and choosing appropriate source types
build a set of keywords and synonyms that drive an effective search
construct and refine a search in a library discovery service using Boolean logic and limiters.

title: In real academic practice
body: Searching well underpins almost everything you do at university. Every essay, report and project begins with finding the right sources, and a strong search saves hours and raises the quality of what you read. Build the craft now and it serves every assignment of your degree, and the research that professional work later asks of you.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons that follow the order of a real search. First, planning your search: the thinking you do before you type. Second, identifying keywords: building the terms that drive the search. Third, searching your discovery service: combining and refining those terms into results you can use. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

The examples and activities in this course use invented people, authors and sources to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, citation or reference you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Orientation
body: You already know what academic searching is and why it matters. This lesson is about the craft: how a good search is planned before you type anything into a box. The difference between a quick search and a productive one is mostly made before the search begins.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level you are building search craft, not learning what a search is. The aim is to plan deliberately: to decide what you are looking for, and what kind of source will answer it, before you start. That planning is what turns a search strategy into more than guesswork.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain why effective searching begins with planning rather than typing terms into a box
set clear search objectives by reflecting on what you already know and what you need
choose appropriate source types and date ranges for a search in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
A search strategy begins with a plan. Before you open a discovery service, you work out what you already know, what you still need to find, and what kind of source will carry the answer. Planning turns a vague topic into a set of search objectives you can act on.

Planning also means choosing the shape of what you are looking for. A current debate needs recent journal articles; a settled definition may come from a textbook; a figure needs a reliable primary source. Deciding source type and date range in advance saves you from sifting results that were never going to fit.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about the last search you ran for your course. Did you plan it, or type a few words and take what came back? What is one thing you could decide in advance next time?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Effective searching is planned, not improvised. Before you open a discovery service you set an objective, decide what kind of source will answer it, and choose a date range to match the task. You can now explain why planning comes first and make those choices for a search of your own. The next lesson builds the keywords that drive the search.

title: Orientation
body: A planned search still needs the right words. Keywords are what you actually type, and they drive everything the search returns. This lesson is about choosing them well: finding the terms that carry your question, and the synonyms that catch what a single word would miss.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You have run searches with keywords before. The craft here is deliberate choice: pulling the core terms out of a question, then widening them with synonyms so the search does not miss relevant work filed under a different word.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: identify the keywords that carry the core of a research question
generate synonyms and alternative terms to broaden or focus a search
assemble a working set of keywords for a search in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Keywords are the words or short phrases you type when you search, and they drive the results: a search can only be as good as the terms you give it. The skill is to find the keywords that carry the core of your question, and to leave out the words that do not help, such as 'effect of' or 'study'.

Most ideas can be named in more than one way, so a single keyword will miss sources that use a different word for the same thing. That is why you also gather synonyms and alternative terms. A good keyword set covers the main concepts of your question and, for each one, the likely ways other authors have named it.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a recent search in your subject. Did you type a sentence or a set of keywords? Which core concept might you have named differently to catch more sources?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Keywords drive a search, so the results can only be as good as the terms you choose. You build a set by pulling the core concepts out of your question, naming each with its best keyword, and widening it with synonyms so the search catches work filed under a different word. You can now assemble a working keyword set of your own. The next lesson combines these terms into a real search.

title: Orientation
body: With a plan and a keyword set ready, you can build the search itself. A library discovery service does far more than a plain search box: it lets you combine terms, search for exact phrases, and narrow results to what you actually need. This lesson is about using those tools.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You have typed keywords into a discovery service before. The craft now is to control it: to join your terms with Boolean logic, tighten them with phrases and wildcards, and apply limiters so the results fit the plan you made.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: combine keywords with Boolean operators (AND, OR, NOT) to control a search
use phrase searching, wildcards and limiters to refine the results
refine a search in {{context}} that returns too many or too few results.

title: Concept: definition
body:
A discovery service lets you combine keywords with Boolean operators. AND narrows a search by requiring both terms; OR widens it by accepting either, which is how you bring in synonyms; NOT excludes a term you do not want. Joining your keywords this way turns a list of words into a controlled search.

Three more tools refine the results. Quotation marks search for an exact phrase, so 'climate change' is treated as one idea. An asterisk is a wildcard that catches word endings, so 'adolescen*' finds adolescent and adolescents. Limiters narrow results by date, source type or availability. Together these tighten a search that returns too much, or loosen one that returns too little.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a search that gave you far too many results, or far too few. Which operator, phrase or limiter from this lesson could you have used to bring it under control?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: A discovery service lets you control a search rather than just run it. You join keywords with AND, OR and NOT, hold phrases together with quotation marks, catch word endings with a wildcard, and narrow with limiters for date and source type. When a search returns too much or too little, you refine it and run it again. You can now construct and refine a search of your own, which is the craft this course set out to build.

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. Searching is no longer something you do by typing a few words and hoping. You can plan a search before you begin, setting an objective and choosing the source type and date range that fit. You can build the keywords and synonyms that drive it. And you can construct and refine a real search in your discovery service, using Boolean operators, phrases, wildcards and limiters to control what comes back. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

title: In real academic practice
body: From here, searching well is something you practise in every module. Each assignment that sends you to the literature, each time you plan before you type, each search you refine rather than abandon, is this craft at work. It is also what research and professional life reward: the ability to find the right evidence quickly, and to know it is the right evidence.

title: Course Sources
instruction: This course draws on the following source.

_items.title: See pages 95 to 112 of Chapter 7, 'Research: Developing Effective Search Strategies', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: The stages of planning a search
body: Planning a search runs through a few ordered steps. Reveal each one to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each step to reveal it. Work through all five in order.

_items.title: Reflect on what you know
_items.body: Start from what you already understand about the topic. Mapping your existing knowledge shows you where the gaps are and what the search actually needs to fill.

_items.title: Set your objective
_items.body: Turn the gap into a clear objective: a specific question or claim you need sources to answer. A sharp objective keeps the whole search focused.

_items.title: Decide the source type
_items.body: Match the objective to a source type. A current debate calls for recent journal articles; a core definition may come from a textbook; figures need a reliable primary source.

_items.title: Set the date range
_items.body: Decide how recent the sources need to be. A fast-moving field needs the last few years; an established idea can draw on older, foundational work.

_items.title: Now open the search
_items.body: Only now do you open the discovery service. With objective, source type and date range decided, the search itself becomes quick and productive.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: Building a keyword set
body: Four moves that turn a question into a working set of keywords.
instruction: Read through the cards below.

_items.title: Pull out the concepts
_items.subtitle: Start here
_items.text: Break your question into its two or three core concepts. Each concept, not each word, is what you need keywords for.

_items.title: Find synonyms
_items.subtitle: Widen each concept
_items.text: For every concept, list the other words authors might use. 'Teenager' may also be 'adolescent' or 'young person'.

_items.title: Drop the dead words
_items.subtitle: Focus the search
_items.text: Leave out words that carry no search meaning, such as 'impact', 'study' or 'effect of'. They only add noise to the results.

_items.title: Test and adjust
_items.subtitle: Refine
_items.text: Run the set, see what comes back, and swap in better terms. A keyword set is a draft you improve, not a fixed list.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: The tools of a discovery service
body: Five tools that let you control a search. Open each one to see what it does.
instruction: Select each heading to reveal it. Work through all five.

_items.title: AND, OR, NOT
_items.body: AND requires both terms and narrows the search. OR accepts either and widens it, which is how you add synonyms. NOT drops a term you want to exclude. These three operators do most of the work of controlling a search.

_items.title: Phrase searching
_items.body: Put quotation marks around words that belong together, such as 'young people', so the service searches for the exact phrase rather than the separate words scattered apart.

_items.title: Wildcards
_items.body: An asterisk stands in for word endings. Searching 'therap*' catches therapy, therapies and therapist in one go, so you do not have to list every form yourself.

_items.title: Limiters
_items.body: Narrow the results by date, source type or availability. Limiters are how you apply the source-type and date decisions you made when you planned the search.

_items.title: Too many or too few
_items.body: If a search returns too much, add an AND term, a phrase or a limiter. If it returns too little, add synonyms with OR, or remove a limiter. Refining is normal, not a sign the search went wrong.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students need sources for the same assignment and both begin to search.

{{learner-a}} opens the discovery service and types the essay title straight into the box. Thousands of results come back, so {{learner-a}} skims the first page and picks whatever looks relevant. There was no objective and no plan, so the search returned everything and nothing. This is searching without planning.

{{learner-b}} stops first and plans. What do I already know, and what do I actually need to find? The objective narrows to one clear question. {{learner-b}} decides recent journal articles will answer it best, and sets a date range of the last five years. Only then does the search begin, and the first page of results is already close to usable.

Both students ran a search. {{learner-b}} did the thinking before the search, not during it, and the plan did most of the work.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students need sources for the same question: does social media use affect teenagers' sleep?

{{learner-a}} types the whole question into the search box, word for word. The service treats common words such as 'does' and 'affect' as search terms, and the results are a scattered mix. {{learner-a}} has used a sentence where keywords were needed, so the search had nothing sharp to work with.

{{learner-b}} pulls out the core concepts first: social media, sleep and teenagers. For each one {{learner-b}} lists alternatives, so social media becomes social media or networking sites, sleep becomes sleep or insomnia, and teenagers becomes teenagers or adolescents. The search now covers the idea however authors have named it, and the results are focused and relevant.

Both searched the same question. {{learner-b}} searched with concepts and synonyms, while {{learner-a}} searched with a sentence.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students take the same keyword set into the discovery service to search for work on social media and teenagers' sleep.

{{learner-a}} types all the words in one after another, with spaces between them. The service returns tens of thousands of results, far too many to use, and {{learner-a}} gives up on the later pages. The terms were all there, but nothing told the service how they fit together.

{{learner-b}} joins the terms with operators, grouping the synonyms with OR and the concepts with AND, and putting quotation marks around each phrase. The wildcards catch the word endings, and the result is a few hundred focused hits. When even that feels broad, {{learner-b}} adds a date limiter for the last five years and the set becomes manageable.

Both used the same keywords. {{learner-b}} told the service how they fit together, then refined from there.

title: Practical guidance
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: Use these questions on your next search.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I written down what I already know about the topic?
Have I turned my gap into a specific objective or question?
Have I decided what kind of source will answer it best?
Have I set a sensible date range for the task?
Have I chosen my starting keywords before opening the search box?
Have I planned the search rather than typing and hoping?

title: Practical guidance
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: Use these questions on your next search.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I broken my question into its core concepts?
Have I picked the keyword that best names each concept?
Have I listed synonyms and alternative terms for each one?
Have I removed common words that carry no search meaning?
Have I covered each main concept of the question at least once?
Am I ready to combine these terms into a search?

title: Practical guidance
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: Use these questions on your next search.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I joined my core concepts with AND to narrow the search?
Have I grouped synonyms with OR so the search catches each form?
Have I put quotation marks around any phrase that belongs together?
Have I used a wildcard to catch word endings where it helps?
Have I applied limiters for date, source type or availability?
If the results were too many or too few, have I adjusted and run it again?

title: Formative check: why planning comes first
displayTitle: Why does effective searching begin with planning rather than typing terms into a search box?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why does effective searching begin with planning?

_items.text: Because the key decisions, what you need and what source will answer it, are made before you search.
_items.feedback: Yes. Planning decides the objective, source type and date range before the search begins.

_items.text: Because the search box is often broken until you plan around it.
_items.feedback: The search box works fine; planning is about your decisions, not the tool.

_items.text: Because planning lets you avoid using keywords altogether.
_items.feedback: Planning does not replace keywords; it decides what the keywords should look for.

_items.text: Because a longer search always finds more sources.
_items.feedback: Length is not the point; a planned search finds better sources, not just more.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The decisions that make a search productive are made in the planning, before you type.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about where a search is really decided: in the planning, or at the search box?
_incorrect.final: Effective searching begins with planning because the objective, source type and date range are decided before you type. The box works; what matters is the thinking you bring to it.

title: Formative check: planning before searching
displayTitle: In the worked example, what did the second student do before starting to search?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What did the second student do before searching?

_items.text: Set a clear objective and chose a source type and date range to fit it.
_items.feedback: Yes. The second student planned the search before opening the discovery service.

_items.text: Typed the essay title straight into the search box.
_items.feedback: That was the first student, searching without a plan.

_items.text: Skimmed the first page of results and picked whatever looked relevant.
_items.feedback: That is the unplanned approach the first student took.

_items.text: Read every result the search returned before choosing.
_items.feedback: The second student narrowed the search first, so there was no need to read everything.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second student planned: a clear objective, then a matching source type and date range.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the second student decided before the search, not during it.
_incorrect.final: Before searching, the second student set an objective and chose a source type and date range. Typing the title or skimming results is the unplanned approach.

title: Formative check: choosing source type and date
displayTitle: You are planning a search for a current debate in {{context}}. Which choice of source type and date range fits best?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which source type and date range fit a current debate?

_items.text: Recent journal articles from the last few years.
_items.feedback: Yes. A live debate in {{context}} is best served by recent journal articles.

_items.text: A general textbook chapter from fifteen years ago.
_items.feedback: A dated textbook will miss the current state of the debate.

_items.text: Whatever appears on the first page of results, regardless of date.
_items.feedback: Taking the first page ignores the planning this lesson asks for.

_items.text: A single encyclopedia entry with no date given.
_items.feedback: An undated encyclopedia entry is too general for a current debate.

_feedback.correct: That's right. For a current debate in {{context}}, recent journal articles fit the task.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. A current debate needs current sources; which option matches that?
_incorrect.final: A current debate in {{context}} is best served by recent journal articles. Old textbooks, undated entries or the first page of results do not fit the task.

title: Formative check: turning a question into keywords
displayTitle: What is the best way to turn a research question into search keywords?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is the best way to turn a question into keywords?

_items.text: Pull out the two or three core concepts and name each with a keyword.
_items.feedback: Yes. Keywords should capture the core concepts, not the whole sentence.

_items.text: Type the whole question into the box, word for word.
_items.feedback: A sentence includes dead words that give the search nothing sharp to work with.

_items.text: Use only the longest word in the question.
_items.feedback: Length does not make a word a good keyword; the core concepts do.

_items.text: Search the exact title of your assignment.
_items.feedback: The assignment title is rarely the set of concepts your sources are filed under.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Good keywords capture the core concepts of the question, not every word in it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which option captures the concepts the question is really about?
_incorrect.final: The best approach is to pull out the core concepts and name each with a keyword. A full sentence, the longest word, or the assignment title all give the search the wrong terms.

title: Formative check: why synonyms matter
displayTitle: In the worked example, why did the second student list alternatives such as 'adolescents' alongside 'teenagers'?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why list alternatives alongside the main keyword?

_items.text: So the search catches relevant sources that use a different word for the same idea.
_items.feedback: Yes. Synonyms catch work filed under a different word for the same concept.

_items.text: To make the search return as many results as possible.
_items.feedback: The aim is relevant results, not simply more of them.

_items.text: Because the first keyword is always the wrong one.
_items.feedback: The first keyword is often fine; synonyms widen it, they do not replace it.

_items.text: To avoid having to use Boolean operators later.
_items.feedback: Synonyms and operators work together; one does not remove the need for the other.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Authors name the same idea in different ways, so synonyms stop the search missing relevant work.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what a single word would miss when authors name an idea differently.
_incorrect.final: The second student listed synonyms so the search would catch sources using a different word for the same idea. It is about relevance, not sheer quantity.

title: Formative check: assembling a keyword set
displayTitle: You are assembling keywords for a search in {{context}}. Which set is most likely to drive an effective search?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which keyword set is most likely to drive an effective search?

_items.text: The core concepts of your question, each with a couple of synonyms.
_items.feedback: Yes. Core concepts plus synonyms is the keyword set this lesson builds for {{context}}.

_items.text: The full research question typed as one long phrase.
_items.feedback: A long phrase includes dead words and gives the search nothing sharp.

_items.text: A single broad word that covers the whole topic.
_items.feedback: One broad word is too vague to focus a search in {{context}}.

_items.text: Every word in the assignment brief, in order.
_items.feedback: Most of the brief's words are not the concepts your sources are filed under.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, a set of core concepts each widened with synonyms drives an effective search.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which option names the concepts and widens them, rather than a sentence or a single word?
_incorrect.final: An effective keyword set for {{context}} is the core concepts, each with a couple of synonyms. A long phrase, one broad word, or the whole brief all search poorly.

title: Formative check: combining synonyms
displayTitle: Which Boolean operator combines two synonyms so the search accepts either one?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which operator combines two synonyms so the search accepts either?

_items.text: OR.
_items.feedback: Yes. OR widens a search by accepting either term, which is how you add synonyms.

_items.text: AND.
_items.feedback: AND requires both terms, which narrows rather than widens the search.

_items.text: NOT.
_items.feedback: NOT excludes a term; it does not combine synonyms.

_items.text: A date limiter.
_items.feedback: A limiter narrows by date; it does not combine synonyms.

_feedback.correct: That's right. OR accepts either synonym, so the search catches both forms.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which operator means 'either of these terms will do'?
_incorrect.final: OR combines synonyms by accepting either term. AND narrows, NOT excludes, and a limiter filters by date or type.

title: Formative check: refining an oversized search
displayTitle: In the worked example, what did the second student do to cut tens of thousands of results down to a usable set?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: How did the second student cut the results down?

_items.text: Joined the terms with operators and phrases, then added a date limiter.
_items.feedback: Yes. Operators, phrases and a limiter turned a flood of results into a focused set.

_items.text: Read further into the later pages of results.
_items.feedback: Reading on does not reduce the results; it only takes longer.

_items.text: Removed the keywords and searched the topic name alone.
_items.feedback: A single broad term would widen the search, not focus it.

_items.text: Searched the same words again in a different order.
_items.feedback: Order alone does not tell the service how the terms fit together.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second student combined the terms with operators and phrases, then narrowed with a limiter.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the moves that told the service how the terms fit together and narrowed the set.
_incorrect.final: The second student used operators and phrases to combine the terms, then a date limiter to narrow. Reading on, dropping keywords or reordering would not focus the search.

title: Formative check: too few results
displayTitle: You run a search in {{context}} and get only a handful of results. Which refinement is most likely to help?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which refinement helps when a search returns too few results?

_items.text: Add synonyms joined with OR, or remove a limiter.
_items.feedback: Yes. Widening with OR synonyms or lifting a limiter brings back more results in {{context}}.

_items.text: Add another AND term to the search.
_items.feedback: Another AND term narrows further, which gives you even fewer results.

_items.text: Put more of the words in quotation marks.
_items.feedback: More exact phrases tighten the search, so the results shrink further.

_items.text: Add a stricter date limiter.
_items.feedback: A stricter limiter removes results; here you need to widen, not narrow.

_feedback.correct: That's right. When a search in {{context}} returns too little, widen it with OR synonyms or by lifting a limiter.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Too few results means the search is too narrow; which option widens it?
_incorrect.final: With too few results in {{context}}, widen the search: add OR synonyms or remove a limiter. Adding AND terms, phrases or stricter limiters only narrows it further.

body: A productive search is mostly decided at which point?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A productive search is mostly decided at which point?

_items.text: Before searching, when you set the objective, source type and date range.
_items.feedback: Yes. The planning decides most of what a search returns.

_items.text: While skimming the first page of results.
_items.feedback: Skimming results is not planning; the decisions come earlier.

_items.text: After downloading everything that looks relevant.
_items.feedback: Collecting everything is the opposite of a planned search.

_items.text: When you give up and borrow a friend's sources.
_items.feedback: That skips searching altogether.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A search is mostly decided in the planning, before you type.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about where the decisions that shape a search are really made.

body: You need sources for a fast-moving current debate. Which plan fits best?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which plan fits a fast-moving current debate?

_items.text: Recent journal articles from the last few years.
_items.feedback: Yes. Current debates need current, peer-reviewed work.

_items.text: A general textbook chapter from fifteen years ago.
_items.feedback: A dated textbook misses the current state of the debate.

_items.text: Whatever appears first, regardless of date.
_items.feedback: Ignoring date abandons the plan.

_items.text: A single undated encyclopedia entry.
_items.feedback: Too general and undated for a live debate.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A current debate is best served by recent journal articles.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. A current debate needs current sources.

body: What is the best way to turn a research question into search terms?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is the best way to turn a question into search terms?

_items.text: Pull out the core concepts and name each with a keyword.
_items.feedback: Yes. Keywords capture the concepts, not the whole sentence.

_items.text: Type the whole question, word for word, into the box.
_items.feedback: A sentence carries dead words that blur the search.

_items.text: Use only the longest word in the question.
_items.feedback: Length does not make a good keyword.

_items.text: Search the assignment title exactly as written.
_items.feedback: The title is rarely the concepts your sources are filed under.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Pull out the core concepts and give each one a keyword.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which option captures the concepts rather than the sentence?

body: Why would you add synonyms such as 'adolescent' alongside 'teenager'?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why add synonyms alongside a main keyword?

_items.text: To catch relevant sources that use a different word for the same idea.
_items.feedback: Yes. Synonyms stop the search missing work filed under another word.

_items.text: To make the search return as many results as possible.
_items.feedback: The aim is relevance, not sheer quantity.

_items.text: To replace the need for Boolean operators.
_items.feedback: Synonyms and operators work together.

_items.text: Because longer searches always find better sources.
_items.feedback: Length alone does not improve a search.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Synonyms catch sources that name the same idea differently.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what a single word would miss.

body: Which Boolean operator combines two synonyms so the search accepts either term?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which operator combines two synonyms so the search accepts either?

_items.text: OR.
_items.feedback: Yes. OR widens a search by accepting either term.

_items.text: AND.
_items.feedback: AND requires both terms, which narrows the search.

_items.text: NOT.
_items.feedback: NOT excludes a term rather than combining synonyms.

_items.text: A wildcard.
_items.feedback: A wildcard catches word endings; it does not combine terms.

_feedback.correct: That's right. OR accepts either synonym.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which operator means 'either term will do'?

body: A search returns tens of thousands of results. Which move narrows it?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which move narrows a search that returns too many results?

_items.text: Add an AND term, a phrase in quotation marks, or a limiter.
_items.feedback: Yes. These all tighten an oversized search.

_items.text: Add more synonyms joined with OR.
_items.feedback: OR synonyms widen the search, giving even more results.

_items.text: Remove the date limiter.
_items.feedback: Removing a limiter widens the search further.

_items.text: Read fewer pages of the results.
_items.feedback: Reading fewer pages does not change what the search returns.

_feedback.correct: That's right. AND terms, phrases and limiters all narrow an oversized search.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Too many results means you need to narrow, not widen.

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: planning a search before you begin, building the keywords that drive it, and searching your discovery service. On their own they are three separate skills. This lesson brings them together into one search strategy you can keep using.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are not expected to run a flawless search every time. The aim is to see these three skills as one connected strategy, not separate steps, so it carries on past this course into the rest of your studies.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: connect planning, keywords and discovery-service searching as one search strategy
analyse how planning, keywords and discovery-service searching work as one strategy in a student's searching
apply the three together on a search you run in your {{context}} study

title: Concept: definition
body: A search strategy is these three skills working as one. It is not three separate tasks but a single flow you run each time you need sources: plan the search, build the keywords that drive it, then construct and refine it in your discovery service. The three lessons are the parts of that one strategy.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice, the three skills run as one flow every time you need sources. You plan the search, build the keywords that drive it, then construct and refine it in your discovery service. Done together, they take far less effort than three separate tries, and they find better sources.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a piece of work coming up that will need sources. How will you run this search strategy for it, from planning to keywords to a refined search?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Searching works best when the three skills run as one strategy. You plan the search, build the keywords that drive it, then construct and refine it in your discovery service, and you reuse that flow each time you need sources. It is the whole strategy, not any single step, that finds good sources.

title: The steps as one process
displayTitle: The steps as one process
body: A search strategy runs as one sequence you follow each time you need sources. Select each step to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each step.

_items.title: Plan
_items.body: Set your objective and choose the source type and date range before you start searching.

_items.title: Build keywords
_items.body: Pull out the core concepts and add a synonym for each, so the search catches more of the relevant sources.

_items.title: Construct
_items.body: Combine the terms with AND, OR and NOT in your discovery service to build the search.

_items.title: Refine
_items.body: Adjust your terms and limiters, then run the search again until the results fit your objective.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body: Two students each need sources for the same assignment. Tom types his topic straight into the discovery service and takes the first results, with no plan and no keyword set. Amara plans first, builds keywords with synonyms, then combines and refines them in the service. Running the three skills as one strategy, Amara finds stronger sources in less time.

title: Working with the cycle
displayTitle: Checklist: How to search as one strategy
body: Use these to run your search as one connected strategy, not three separate steps.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Did I plan the search before I started typing?
Did I build keywords and synonyms for each core concept?
Did I combine my terms with AND, OR and NOT?
Did I refine the search when it returned too much or too little?
Can I reuse this strategy the next time I need sources?

displayTitle: Why is it more useful to treat searching as one connected strategy rather than three separate tasks?
body: Why is it more useful to treat searching as one connected strategy rather than three separate tasks?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it more useful to treat searching as one connected strategy rather than three separate tasks?

_items.text: Because each step feeds the next: the plan shapes the keywords, and the keywords shape the search you then refine.
_items.feedback: Yes. The plan drives the keywords, and the keywords drive the search you refine, so the steps work as one.

_items.text: Because planning once means you never have to build keywords or search at all.
_items.feedback: Not so. Planning sets up the keywords and the search; it does not replace them.

_items.text: Because treating the three as separate tasks is always faster than connecting them.
_items.feedback: Separate tasks tend to waste effort, because a weak plan leads to weak keywords and a weak search.

_items.text: Because a discovery service does the planning and keyword work for you.
_items.feedback: A discovery service runs the search, but you still plan it and build the keywords first.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The plan shapes the keywords, the keywords shape the search, and refining feeds back in, so the three work as one strategy.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about how each step sets up the one after it.

displayTitle: A student plans a search, builds keywords with synonyms, then combines and refines them in the discovery service, and finds strong sources quickly. What does this show?
body: A student plans a search, builds keywords with synonyms, then combines and refines them in the discovery service, and finds strong sources quickly. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student plans a search, builds keywords with synonyms, then combines and refines them in the discovery service, and finds strong sources quickly. What does this show?

_items.text: That the three skills work as one strategy: the plan, the keywords and the refined search together found good sources.
_items.feedback: Yes. Each step set up the next, and together they found strong sources.

_items.text: That only the discovery service mattered, and the plan and keywords did not.
_items.feedback: The discovery service worked because the plan and keywords prepared it. All three mattered.

_items.text: That the student was lucky, since good sources come mainly by chance.
_items.feedback: Good sources came from the strategy, not luck: plan, keywords, then a refined search.

_items.text: That planning alone was enough, and the keywords and search added nothing.
_items.feedback: Planning started it, but the keywords and the refined search did the finding too.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The plan, the keywords and the refined search worked together as one strategy.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at how the three steps worked together to find the sources.

displayTitle: You want to use this search strategy to find sources for {{context}} this term. Which plan works best?
body: You want to use this search strategy to find sources for {{context}} this term. Which plan works best?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You want to use this search strategy to find sources for your subject this term. Which plan works best?

_items.text: Plan each search first, build keywords with synonyms, then combine and refine them in the discovery service, every time.
_items.feedback: Yes. That runs the whole strategy, in order, each time you need sources.

_items.text: Type your topic straight into the search box and take whatever comes back.
_items.feedback: That skips the plan, the keywords and the refining. It is the habit this course replaces.

_items.text: Build a long keyword list, but skip planning and never refine the results.
_items.feedback: Keywords alone are not the strategy. The plan sets them up and refining tunes the search.

_items.text: Rely on the discovery service limiters and ignore the plan and keywords.
_items.feedback: Limiters help, but only after a plan and good keywords. They are one part, not the whole.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Planning, keywords, then a refined search, run in order each time, is the whole strategy.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about which plan runs all three skills, in order, each time.
